title: Senate committee delays vote on Todd Blanche attorney general nomination – as it happened
text: This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day, but our colleagues in Australia will continue providing updates on the US-Israel war on Iran. Here are the latest developments in US politics: The Senate judiciary committee has postponed a vote, scheduled for Thursday, on the nomination of Todd Blanche, Donald Trump’s former criminal defense lawyer, to be attorney general. Barack Obama, the former president who installed basketball hoop on the White House tennis court, endorsed the US Senate campaign of Iowa Democrat Josh Turek, a state lawmaker who played wheelchair basketball in four Paralympic Games, winning two gold medals, in a new ad filmed as the two shot hoops. The US Senate unanimously passed a resolution declaring its opposition to any presidential pardon for Ghislaine Maxwell, the longtime Jeffrey Epstein associate who is currently serving a 20-year prison sentence for sex-trafficking crimes. Marjorie Taylor Greene, the former Maga congresswoman, announced on Wednesday that she was married on Tuesday in Las Vegas to another recent exile from Trump’s good graces, Brian Glenn, the self-described “Maga mouthpiece” who quit his job as White House correspondent for the far-right network Real America’s Voice after his fiancee was cast out by the president for supporting the release of the Epstein files and criticizing his bombing of Iran in 2025. Lawyers for former FBI director James Comey have alleged that US Secret Service agents illegally surveilled him, Trump requested regular updates into the investigation, and law enforcement turned to ChatGPT and a known mafia killer as they scrambled to find justification for criminally charging Comey for posting a picture of seashells that spelled out “8647”. Senate Republicans voted on Wednesday to advance as a bloc the nominations of 71 of Donald Trump’s picks to serve in a variety of roles requiring confirmation, including as ambassadors, US attorneys, judges and senior staff at federal agencies. Among the nominees soon to be confirmed this way is P. Wells Griffith, a former Republican campaign operative and Trump aide who was the senior director for international energy and environment on the National Security Council in 2019. During the impeachment inquiry over Trump’s pressure campaign against Ukraine that year, Fiona Hill, the NSC’s Russia expert during Trump’s first term, testified that Griffith was present at a July 2019 meeting with Ukrainian officials in which John Bolton, then Trump’s national security adviser, discovered that other US officials had secretly pressed Ukraine to open a sham investigation of Joe Biden. Griffith is in line to be an ambassador, representing the United States at the International Atomic Energy Agency in Vienna. The IAEA played a key role in verifying Iran’s compliance with the nuclear deal negotiated during the Obama administration, which Trump withdrew from during his first term, and could be similarly important should a new nuclear deal with Iran be struck by the Trump administration after the US-Israeli war on Iran finally ends. Robert Garcia, the senior Democrat on the House oversight committee, issued a scathing statement on the Republican-led Senate judiciary committee postponing a confirmation vote on the nomination of Todd Blanche to be attorney general. “Republicans were forced to postpone Todd Blanche’s confirmation vote because they knew he was too corrupt and untrustworthy to get enough votes,” Garcia said. “Blanche went from being Trump’s personal lawyer to running the Epstein files cover-up and orchestrating billion-dollar slush funds. He is not qualified to be the top law enforcement officer in this country. We will not stop fighting until Donald Trump withdraws his nomination”. Garcia and the senior Democrat on the Senate judiciary committee, Dick Durbin, had urged the Senate to reject Blanche’s nomination over his handling of the Epstein files and “his personal involvement in moving Ghislaine Maxwell to a minimum-security prison.” The US has said it is conducting airstrikes ‌in ‌Iran, after a lull of several days in direct US attacks on targets in Iran. Donald Trump said America would strike Iran hard, telling reporters in the Oval Office on Wednesday: “We’re going to be hitting them very hard, because it’s our turn to hit them. They know it’s coming.” The US military said its attacks were a “powerful response to yesterday’s attempted Iranian attacks on US forces based in the Middle East”. On Wednesday Iran launched a barrage of missiles at American military installations in Jordan – its first attack in the region since the pause in fighting – meanwhile the US partnered with Saudi Arabia to strike Tehran-backed militias in Iraq, killing at least 20 fighters and six Iranian advisers. Elsewhere, drone strikes ignited fires on two natural gas vessels at the Egyptian port of Damietta, according to Ambrey, a British maritime security firm. It was not immediately clear who was responsible for the strikes on a US-owned floating storage facility and a Greek-owned tanker. No injuries were reported. The Senate judiciary committee has postponed a vote, scheduled for Thursday, on the nomination of Todd Blanche, Donald Trump’s former criminal defense lawyer, to be attorney general. Blanche, who holds the role on an acting basis, apparently lacks the votes of two Republican senators who want him to confirm in writing that the Department of Justice will not proceed with a $1.776bn fund to compensate Trump supporters who stormed the Capitol on January 6 2021, or a pledge to forever bar the IRS from investigating the tax returns of the president and his family. The two senators, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Cornyn of Texas, both lost their re-election bids this year in Republican primaries in which Trump backed their opponents. A spokesperson for the committee, which is chaired by Iowa Republican Chuck Grassley said in a statement: “Chairman Grassley works to set President Trump’s nominees up for success in committee, not failure. Senators Cornyn and Tillis want written assurances from the Department of Justice regarding the Trump-IRS settlement. Tomorrow’s markup is postponed as work continues to secure sufficient support in committee to favorably report Attorney General-nominee Todd Blanche, who is highly qualified for the job.” In a new ad released on Wednesday, Barack Obama, the former president who installed basketball hoop on the White House tennis court, endorsed the US Senate campaign of Iowa Democrat Josh Turek, a state lawmaker who played wheelchair basketball in four Paralympic Games, winning two gold medals. The ad shows the two men talking about Obama’s win in the 2008 Iowa caucuses, and Turek’s hope to flip a Republican-held Senate seat in the upcoming midterms as they shoot hoops, playing a modified game of Horse called I-O-W-A. Obama’s temporary conversion of the White House tennis court into a place to shoot hoops was recently mocked by his successor, Donald Trump, in an appearance on a podcast to encourage children to read, Storytime with the Second Lady. In the podcast episode, released over the Fourth of July weekend, Trump read, and commented on, an illustreated children’s book called President’s Play, about the sporting activities of presidents through the years. When he came to a part of the book that showed Jimmy Carter playing on the White House tennis court, and the text on the next page read, “President Barack Obama used the same court for basketball”, Trump said instead: “Barack Hussein Obama, he used the same court for basketball”. “There’s a picture of each,” he added. “Jimmy as a tennis player. Barack Hussein Obama as a basketball player. I don’t know if he’s a good basketball player. I tend to doubt it. Actually, his favorite sport is golf.” When the second lady, Usha Vance, replied, “Oh, is that right?” Trump added another gratuitous dig, with a perhaps racist undertone: “Yeah. But he won’t be in the Masters anytime soon.” Trump, who mentioned Obama’s Arabic middle name an average of once a year during his first three years as president, has seemed obsessed with pronouncing the name at every opportunity during his second term, almost treating it like an insulting nickname. A review of speech transcripts and remarks reveals that, in the past six months, Trump has referred to Obama by his full name 60 times, including in those comments addressed at children. On multiple occasions, Trump has credited Rush Limbaugh, the influential far-right radio host he gave a Presidential Medal of Freedom to before his death, with coming up with the idea to use Obama’s middle name as a kind of slur. The US Senate on Wednesday unanimously passed a resolution declaring its opposition to any presidential pardon for Ghislaine Maxwell, the longtime Jeffrey Epstein associate who is currently serving a 20-year prison sentence for sex-trafficking crimes. Introduced by Senator Jacky Rosen, a Democrat of Nevada, the resolution states that Maxwell “should not be granted a Presidential pardon or any form of clemency for her crimes with Jeffrey Epstein relating to the sexual exploitation and abuse of minors”. Although Senate resolutions like these are non-binding and symbolic, Rosen’s office noted in a news release in February when she introduced the measure that the resolution was “designed to put the Senate on record opposing the prospect” of Donald Trump of granting a pardon or clemency to Maxwell. “It’s frankly horrifying that Trump would entertain the idea of clemency for even a second for a convicted sex trafficker,” Rosen said in a floor speech on Wednesday. The resolution was brought on Wednesday, as the Senate weighed Trump’s nomination of Todd Blanche, the acting attorney general, to stay in the role permanently. Rosen said its unanimous passage sent a clear message to the White House and Blanche that “there should be NO special treatment for Ghislaine Maxwell”. Marjorie Taylor Greene, the former Maga congresswoman, announced on Wednesday that she was married on Tuesday in Las Vegas to another recent exile from Donald Trump’s good graces, Brian Glenn, the self-described “Maga mouthpiece” who quit his job as White House correspondent for the far-right network Real America’s Voice after his fiancee was cast out by the president for supporting the release of the Epstein files and criticizing his bombing of Iran in 2025. Glenn, who announced his resignation on the air in May, had previously been an openly partisan supporter of Trump, even on the job, mixing praise for the president into his questions for him, which were often phrased to help Trump push his talking points. Before Trump’s rift with Greene, he had eagerly called on Glenn at Oval Office events, using him as a lifeline to avoid potentially awkward or challenging questions from non-partisan reporters. Glenn’s most memorable intervention was his decision to ramp up the pressure on Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, during a tension-filled Oval Office meeting with Trump last year by asking the visiting wartime president why he was in military attire rather than a suit. “Why don’t you wear a suit? You’re at the highest level in this country’s office and you refuse to wear a suit,” Glenn asked Zelenskyy. While Glenn is no longer in the White House press pack, he has been replaced by a group of similarly partisan rightwing correspondents Trump can call on in the Oval Office for help in pursuing his political agenda. In the recently concluded Oval Office event on Wednesday, for example, Trump called in quick succession on: Elizabeth Troutman Mitchell, a correspondent for the far-right Daily Signal, a news site started by the conservative Heritage Foundation, who asked Trump if Dr Anthony Fauci “should face repercussions” for invoking his Fifth Amendment right not to answer questions at Rand Paul’s conspiratorial questions on Wednesday; Cara Castronuova, a former fitness influencer now working for the far-right outlet Lindell TV, who asked Trump to opine on former president Joe Biden’s alleged use of an autopen to sign a preemptive pardon of Fauci; and Bev Turner, a pro-Trump correspondent for the far-right British outlet GB News, whose questions on the new UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, gave Trump an opportunity to repeat his well-known opposition to windmills and advocacy of increased North Sea oil drilling, and then his claim that immigration “is killing your country”. At the end of the event, as the correspondents filed out of the Oval Office, Trump shouted to the GB News correspondent, who recently conducted a fawning interview with him, “Thank you, Bev!” Todd Blanche’s hopes of becoming US attorney general seemed to be in jeopardy on Wednesday after the Department of Justice did not provide written assurances to a key Republican senator that a $1.8bn slush fund was dead. The US Senate judiciary committee will hold a vote on Thursday on whether to advance Blanche’s nomination. Blanche, Trump’s former personal lawyer, is already serving as acting US attorney general. He needs the vote of every Republican on the Senate judiciary panel to advance his nomination to land the role on a permanent basis. But a swing vote on the committee, John Cornyn of Texas, told reporters on Wednesday he would not support Blanche’s nomination until he received written confirmation that the fund was not moving ahead. Cornyn also wants to clarify that a provision giving the president, his sons and related businesses blanket immunity from tax audits for all matters up until this year could not be applied to future matters, or to people who were not parties to the settlement. “Maybe they think I’m just going to give up or, you know, go along, but they’re mistaken,” said Cornyn, a four-term Republican senator who lost a re-election bid earlier this year to a Trump-endorsed rival. “We actually sent them a red-line strikeout of what we need, and they just need to make a decision. And if they do, then we’ll proceed with the markup tomorrow.” Near the end of his Oval Office exchange with reporters on Wednesday, Donald Trump was asked by Jacqui Heinrich of Fox News if he wants the House to come back before 31 August “to act on the Russian and Iran sanctions bill” named for the late Lindsey Graham that advanced in the Senate on Tuesday. Trump said he wanted one change in the Senate bill. “I’d like them to add Iran as tariffs, not just as sanctions. I think it’s important, that’s what Lindsey wanted, because I heard that they have tariffs on Russia but not on … countries with, having to do with Iran. I’d like to see tariffs on Iran. That would make it much stronger,” Trump said. “Perhaps, you’re very good at this, you can maybe tell them,” Trump added, openly suggesting that the correspondent for the rightwing network, who is also married to a Republican congressman, might be willing to lobby lawmakers on his behalf. As we reported on Tuesday, a number of Democrats are alarmed that the Senate legislation, as currently written, gives the president vast new authority to impose sanctions on any nation he deems to have facilitated the purchase of Russian oil. One of them, senator Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire, explained last night that she voted against advancing the Senate bill because “today’s bill gives the President new authority to impose tariffs, even on our allies. I do not think tariffs, which are paid for by American businesses and consumers, will help Ukraine win this war. And over the last year, it’s become more clear that President Trump will use any legal — or illegal — mechanism to make families pay his reckless tariffs.” “I fully support the goal of sanctioning Russia and its enablers and hope that we can have a meaningful amendment process so that I can support the final bill,” Hassan added. Trump also told reporters he ⁠would like ‌Congress to add tariffs on Iran to ‌Russia sanctions legislation that was being ⁠pushed by senator Lindsey Graham before he died ‌recently. I’d like them to add Iran as tariffs, not just as sanctions. I think it’s important. That’s what Lindsey wanted, because I heard that they have tariffs on Russia, but not on those five countries with having to do with Iran. I’d like to see tariffs on Iran. It would make it much stronger. Trump also said that Britain’s new prime minister ⁠Andy Burnham told ‌him he ‌planned to open up the North Sea ‌to oil development, a move that would ⁠mark a shift in the country’s energy policy. The US president rambled through his usual criticisms of the UK, from immigration to windmills, before concluding that the UK will “be a rich country again” if it opens up the North Sea to oil exploration. Speaking in the Oval Office just now, Trump reiterated his threat that ⁠the ⁠United States would hit Iran very ⁠hard. He said he was briefed on a drone ‌attack on tankers off Egypt. “It’s a little more of the same, but it’s going to be straightening out,” Trump said. “In the meantime, we’re going to be hitting them very hard, because it’s our turn to hit them,” Trump told reporters. “They know it’s coming.” He said Washington would see if ‌there was an agreement at some point, “but we’re going to hit them very ⁠hard”. Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu ⁠explored all possible paths to curb Iran’s nuclear program in their White House meeting yesterday, including diplomacy, economic pressure and force, a senior Israeli official has told Reuters. Netanyahu did not tell Trump that Israel’s preference ⁠now was for further attacks on Iran, the official said in briefings with reporters after the meeting. “In the end, it’s his decision,” the official, speaking ⁠on condition of anonymity, said of Trump. The US president has three options and all were discussed at length, said the official, listing them as “a [negotiated] deal, continuing the blockade and economic ‌pressures, and a massive strike.” Netanyahu also ‌added unspecified new ideas to the mix, the official added. Trump had voiced irritation with the Israeli prime minister ahead of their meeting, complaining ‌that details had surfaced publicly about Netanyahu’s plans to talk about new intelligence on Pickaxe Mountain, a deep-underground, nuclear-linked facility that Trump has threatened to bomb. Pushing back against any notion of tensions over the issue, the official said the two allies readily share intelligence, denied that Netanyahu had pushed Trump to escalate militarily against Iran and left open the possibility of a diplomatic solution. At the same time, the Israeli official acknowledged that Trump is the “senior partner” while ‌Netanyahu is the “junior partner” in the allies’ conflict with Iran. Donald Trump and the justice department are asking the US supreme court to toss an $83m defamation verdict won by writer E Jean Carroll after she accused him of sexual assault, saying he cannot be sued for comments he made while he was president. It is the second time Trump has asked the justices to nix damages awarded by a jury to Carroll, a longtime New York advice columnist and former talkshow host. The supreme court refused in June to hear his appeal of another verdict, for $5m, that found him liable for sexual abuse and defamation, the Associated Press reports. The latest case centers on comments Trump made during his first term as US president. The justice department wants to invoke the Westfall Act, which shields government employees from being sued for doing their jobs. “Absent this Court’s intervention, the sitting President is facing nearly a hundred million dollars of personal liability for conduct that was well within the scope of his federal office,” federal attorneys wrote. “That alone deserves this Court’s attention.” The appeal was filed electronically and is expected to be formally docketed with the court on Wednesday. Donald Trump is due to announce a $22bn plan to rebuild Washington’s Dulles international airport today after he personally weighed in on the design of the capital’s main international gateway. A White House official confirmed an announcement would be made, after CBS News reported that Trump had scrutinized 3D models from contractors competing to carry out the overhaul at the White House, and offered proposed changes. An announcement is scheduled for 3pm ET at the White House, where Trump will be joined by Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, Scott Kirby, United Airlines chief executive, and officials from the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority (MWAA), which operates the airport under a 50-year lease from Congress. The planned overhaul of Dulles forms part of a broader pattern of Trump personally directing changes to Washington, from a proposed White House ballroom to a planned 250ft arch. Unlike some of those projects, the president’s push to remake Dulles has drawn a more tepid response, given longstanding complaints about the airport’s distance from the city, its jet-fuel-scented concourses, and its reliance on ageing shuttle vehicles. The scheme is expected to include five new terminals to replace the airport’s existing four, with the underground train system expanded so passengers no longer need Dulles’s much-maligned “mobile lounges” – the slow-moving shuttles that ferry travelers across the tarmac to their gates. A new underground pedestrian tunnel and additional moving walkways are also planned. People briefed on the proposal said the approved design leans on glass and gold, including gold-mirrored ceilings throughout the terminals. United, which handles roughly 70% of traffic at Dulles, has agreed to help finance the project, which is expected to take years and cost more than $20bn, according to the Washington Post. MWAA is expected to fund much of the work through new bond issuances, and had already approved a separate $7bn capital plan for the airport in 2025. United and MWAA did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Trump has made no secret of his dissatisfaction with the airport, telling reporters in December that Dulles “should be a great airport” but “it’s a terrible airport”. The Senate was due to vote today on the latest Iran war powers resolution at 3.30pm ET, less than a week after it voted down efforts to curb Donald Trump’s military action in Iran. However, Politico hears that the vote could be delayed to tomorrow due to GOP “attendance issues”. Indeed, several Republican senators including South Carolinians Tim Scott and Darline Graham are due to attend the funeral for the late senator Lindsey Graham in their home state. And with Mitch McConnell still recovering at home from last month’s fall, the three absences will eat into the majority’s numbers, Politico notes. Last month, the upper chamber delivered a symbolic but significant rebuke to Trump’s deeply unpopular conflict when it approved a war powers resolution preventing the president from continuing hostilities against Iran. That resolution passed by a 50-48 vote, with four Republicans – Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Bill Cassidy of Louisiana and Rand Paul of Kentucky – breaking with their party to support its adoption. John Fetterman, of Pennsylvania, was the sole Democrat to vote against the resolution. The absences of two Republicans, Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania and McConnell of Kentucky, who was admitted to the hospital the week prior, also helped its passage. But last week’s resolution failed by a vote of 49-47 after Fetterman joined Republicans once again, while Collins joined Democrats. It marked the 12th time the Senate has attempted to pass legislation limiting Trump’s ability to attack Iran. The House, meanwhile, has twice passed such measures to direct Trump to withdraw the US military from the conflict. Democrats have been forcing votes regularly since Trump launched his war against Iran with Israel on 28 February. As noted above, though, the resolutions are largely symbolic, and Trump has continued to attack Iran regardless. But they do serve to force lawmakers to go on the record with their stance on the war – which has exacerbated the US cost-of-living and affordability crisis – as November’s midterm elections creep ever closer.
